lesson.title: Jefferson Tries to Reconcile a Divided Republic
lesson.summary: After the bitter election of 1800, Jefferson's presidency promoted an agrarian vision of limited government and reduced federal power, even as his own record of stretching constitutional limits and owning enslaved people complicated that philosophy.
lesson.body:
When Thomas Jefferson took the oath of office in March 1801, becoming president after the bitter, deadlocked election of 1800, he used his inaugural address to try to calm a nation that had just lived through its first real experience of partisan combat. He told the country that despite the fierce contest just concluded, Americans shared common republican principles beneath their party labels, an attempt to lower the political temperature after years of conflict stretching back to his own clashes with Hamilton over the national bank and the Alien and Sedition Acts fight of the Adams years.

Jefferson's vision of government, often called Jeffersonian Democracy, rested on the belief that the United States should remain primarily a republic of independent farmers, what he called yeoman farmers, who owned their own land and were therefore free from the kind of economic dependence that Jefferson believed made people vulnerable to political corruption. He distrusted large cities, banks, and concentrated manufacturing, seeing them as breeding grounds for the same inequality and factionalism he associated with European societies, and he continued to favor a strict reading of the Constitution that limited the federal government's reach.

In practice, Jefferson governed somewhat less radically than his earlier rhetoric suggested. He kept much of Hamilton's financial system in place, including the Bank of the United States he had once argued was unconstitutional, but worked with his Treasury Secretary, Albert Gallatin, to sharply reduce the national debt, shrink the military, and eliminate unpopular internal taxes like the whiskey excise that had provoked the Whiskey Rebellion under Washington. He also allowed the Alien and Sedition Acts to expire and pardoned those who had been convicted under the Sedition Act, undoing what he saw as the worst excesses of the Adams administration.

Jefferson's presidency also revealed real tensions within his own philosophy. His commitment to a strictly limited federal government and to individual liberty coexisted, sometimes uneasily, with his continued ownership of enslaved people at Monticello and with his willingness, as the coming Louisiana Purchase would show, to stretch his own strict constructionist principles when a larger national opportunity was at stake. These contradictions did not go unnoticed by contemporaries and remain central to how historians evaluate his legacy today.

Despite these tensions, Jeffersonian Democracy left a lasting mark on American political culture, establishing an enduring suspicion of centralized financial and political power, a rhetorical commitment to the common farmer and ordinary citizen over elite interests, and a party, the Democratic-Republicans, that would dominate national politics for the next quarter century. The philosophy Jefferson articulated in 1801 would soon be tested by the practical demands of governing an expanding nation, nowhere more dramatically than in the negotiations that produced the Louisiana Purchase just two years into his presidency.
